hook.line: Vale keeps asking when the café will really be theirs, and nobody can say. When you talk about something that hasn't happened yet, Spanish changes the verb after *cuando*. It is the same vowel switch you already know.
hook.es: Cuando el café sea nuestro, vamos a cambiar el menú.
hook.en: When the café is ours, we're going to change the menu.

rule:
English hides this one. *When you get here* looks like the present, even though it is about later. Spanish shows it.

When *cuando* points to something that hasn't happened yet, the verb after it takes the other vowel: *-ar* verbs take *e*, *-er* and *-ir* verbs take *a*. *Llegar* gives *llegues*, *terminar* gives *termine*, and the irregular ones you know come along: *sepa*, *tengamos*, *sea*, *salga*.

The same goes for *en cuanto* (as soon as) and *hasta que* (until).

The test: is it still in the future? Then use this form. The other half of the sentence is usually a future, a command or the plain present: *llámame*, *te aviso*, *empezamos*.
smallPrint: Teachers call this the subjunctive in time clauses. What matters is not whether you know the date, only whether it has happened yet.

yourTurn.prompt: Choose *llegas* or *llegues* and type the whole sentence: Cuando ___, llámame. (When you get here, call me. To a friend.)
yourTurn.why: It hasn't happened yet, so *cuando* takes the other vowel: *llegues*.

yourTurn.prompt: Choose *sé* or *sepa* and type the whole sentence: En cuanto ___ algo, te aviso. (As soon as I know anything, I'll let you know.)
yourTurn.answer: En cuanto sepa algo, te aviso.
accept: Te aviso en cuanto sepa algo.
yourTurn.why: It is still in the future, so you need the other vowel: *sepa*.

yourTurn.prompt: Say: When Vale gets here, we'll start.
yourTurn.why: Vale's arrival is still to come, so *llegue*.

yourTurn.prompt: Tell a friend: Wait until the lawyer gets here.
yourTurn.answer: Espera hasta que llegue la abogada.
accept: Espera hasta que la abogada llegue.
yourTurn.why: *Hasta que* about the future works the same way: *llegue*.

yourTurn.prompt: Say: When we have the money, we'll buy the building.
yourTurn.answer: Cuando tengamos plata, compramos el edificio.
accept: Cuando tengamos la plata, compramos el edificio.
Compramos el edificio cuando tengamos plata.
yourTurn.why: *Tenemos* becomes *tengamos* when the money is still to come.

yourTurn.prompt: Change it from a habit to something still to come: *Cuando salgo de la reunión, te llamo.* (When I get out of the meeting, I'll call you.)
yourTurn.answer: Cuando salga de la reunión, te llamo.
yourTurn.why: Only the verb after *cuando* changes: *salgo* becomes *salga*.

yourTurn.prompt: Ask a friend: What are you going to do when you finish?
yourTurn.why: Finishing is still ahead, so *termines*, the *-ar* verb with an *e*.

pitfalls.why: Almost. *Llegas* is for a habit or a fact. For something still to come, use *llegues*.
English never puts *will* after *when*, and Spanish doesn't put the future there either.

pitfalls.wrong: Espera hasta que llega la abogada.
pitfalls.right: Espera hasta que llegue la abogada.
pitfalls.why: The lawyer hasn't arrived yet, so *hasta que* wants the other vowel.

pitfalls.wrong: Cuando llegue ayer, Vale ya estaba aquí.
pitfalls.right: Cuando llegué ayer, Vale ya estaba aquí.
pitfalls.why: Yesterday has already happened, so use the ordinary past. The accent makes *llegué* (I arrived) different from *llegue*.

personal: Say something true about your own near future with *cuando* or *en cuanto*.
